# Finite center-graph tensorization and an exact local-budget obstruction

This note proves a finite tensorization lemma with an explicit geometric
compatibility condition. It then disproves a proposed automatic way of
meeting the needed local-depth budget. Neither statement establishes or
refutes unconditional mixed-integer tensorization.

## 1. A finite center-graph tensorization lemma

Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and finite. Its relative Helly
number \(h(P)\) is the smallest positive integer \(h\) such that every
finite family of closed convex sets whose intersection misses \(P\)
has a subfamily of at most \(h\) already missing \(P\).

For each \(z\in P\), let \(\sigma_z\) be a finite positive Borel measure
on \(\mathbb R^d\), of mass \(w_z\), supported on an allowed fiber
\(K_z\), and choose a point \(c_z\in K_z\). Zero masses are allowed, but put
\(W=\sum_z w_z>0\). Suppose there is a common \(\kappa\in(0,1]\) such that
\[
 \sigma_z(J)\ge\kappa w_z
 \quad\hbox{for every closed continuous halfspace }J\ni c_z. \tag{1}
\]
For zero masses the condition is automatic. In zero continuous dimension
use the analogous trivial statement with \(\kappa=1\).

Assume the center map respects every convex representation landing in
\(P\):
\[
 z=\sum_{v\in P}\lambda_v v,\quad
 \lambda_v\ge0,\quad\sum_v\lambda_v=1
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 c_z=\sum_v\lambda_v c_v. \tag{2}
\]
In the notation of the recession-space note, each coordinate of the
center map belongs to \(\mathcal L(P)\). This definition makes sense
without assuming that \(P\) is a lattice-convex set.

Define the disjoint fiber measure
\[
 \mu=\sum_{z\in P}\delta_z\otimes\sigma_z.
\]

**Lemma.** Under (1)-(2), there exists one of the chosen fiber centers
\(y=(z_*,c_{z_*})\) such that every closed ambient halfspace containing
\(y\) has mass at least
\[
 \mu(H)\ge\frac{\kappa W}{h(P)}. \tag{3}
\]

*Proof.* Put \(\Gamma=\{(z,c_z):z\in P\}\), and give these graph points
the atomic weights \(w_z\). Condition (2) implies, for each \(A\subset P\),
\[
 \Gamma\cap\operatorname{conv}\{(z,c_z):z\in A\}
   =\{(z,c_z):z\in P\cap\operatorname{conv}A\}. \tag{4}
\]
Projection gives the forward inclusion, and (2) applied to a convex
representation using \(A\) gives the reverse inclusion.

A subset of a finite set is the trace of a closed convex set precisely
when it equals its relative convex-hull closure. Equation (4) therefore
identifies the convex-set traces on \(\Gamma\) with those on \(P\).
Their relative Helly numbers agree.

The elementary weighted Helly centerpoint argument gives a graph point
\(y\) for which every closed ambient halfspace containing \(y\) captures
graph weight at least \(W/h(P)\). To check this argument with boundary
atoms, normalize \(W=1\) and intersect all closed halfspaces of weight
greater than \(1-1/h(P)\). Any at most \(h(P)\) of them have positive
intersection weight, by the union bound. Helly and finiteness of the
graph give a common graph point. A closed halfspace through that point
of weight less than \(1/h(P)\) would have an open complement of weight
greater than \(1-1/h(P)\). Move a closed complementary parallel halfspace
slightly inside the open complement, retaining all its finitely many
graph points. It contradicts the selected common point.

Now fix any ambient closed halfspace \(H\) containing the selected \(y\).
For each graph point \((z,c_z)\in H\), its continuous slice \(H_z\)
contains \(c_z\). If the continuous component of the normal is nonzero,
this slice is a closed halfspace and (1) applies. If that component is
zero, the slice is the whole continuous space, so the same lower bound
holds. Consequently
\[
 \mu(H)=\sum_z\sigma_z(H_z)
 \ge\kappa\sum_{(z,c_z)\in H}w_z
 \ge\frac{\kappa W}{h(P)}.
\]
The chosen point is a single point in an actual allowed fiber. No
orientation restriction, rounding, or interchange of infima was used.
This proves (3). \(\square\)

## 2. Uniform convex fibers

Suppose \(K_z\) are actual convex fibers and \(\sigma_z\) are their
\(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue measures. For positive-volume fibers use
their ordinary centroids. Grünbaum's classical theorem gives (1) with
\(\kappa=\gamma_d\). Thus, if these centroids satisfy (2),
\[
 \max_{y\in S}\operatorname{depth}_{\mu}(y)
       \ge\frac{\gamma_d}{h(P)}. \tag{5}
\]
For a finite lattice-convex projection of affine rank \(r\), Doignon's
theorem gives \(h(P)\le2^r\), and hence the desired factor
\(\gamma_d/2^r\) within this class.

The same argument handles intrinsic measure. If the largest fiber
dimension is \(q\), only its \(q\)-dimensional fibers carry positive
\(\mathcal H_q\)-mass. Their intrinsic centroids have local factor
\(\gamma_q\ge\gamma_d\); the other fibers may be given arbitrary
centers consistent with (2) and have weight zero. Closed halfspaces
whose boundaries contain an entire positive-mass affine fiber cause
no difficulty: that fiber contributes its entire mass.

Condition (2) permits different fiber shapes. It holds, for example,
for an affine centroid section, and for any nonaffine centroid section
in \(\mathcal L(P)\). This is more general than a product family. It is
an actual assumption: convexity of the full body does not force it.

One may use unequal local factors by replacing \(w_z\) in the atomic
graph by a certified unnormalized local-depth weight \(t_z\), where
\(\sigma_z(J)\ge t_z\) for every \(J\ni c_z\). The identical proof yields
\[
 \mu(H)\ge\frac{\sum_z t_z}{h(P)}. \tag{6}
\]
The following example shows that maximizing these local weights over
compatible center choices does not automatically provide the full
\(\gamma_d W\) budget needed to deduce (5) from (6).

## 3. An exact obstruction to the compatible local-depth budget

Fix \(d\ge1\), and let
\[
 T=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:x_i\ge0,\ \sum_i x_i\le1\},
 \qquad c=|T|>0.
\]
Choose \(2^{-1/d}<\rho<1\). Put
\[
 P=\{-1,0,1\},\qquad K_-=K_+=\rho T,\qquad K_0=T,
\]
and take the convex hull of these three fibers. Its exact integer
fibers are the displayed ones, since their endpoint Minkowski midpoint
is \(\rho T\subset T\). Its ambient dimension is \(d+1\), all fibers
have positive \(d\)-volume, and
\[
 M=c(1+2\rho^d).
\]
All three are nonheavy: the middle mass \(c\) is below \(M/2\) because
\(2\rho^d>1\), and each endpoint mass \(\rho^d c\) is below \(M/2\)
automatically.

Here \(\mathcal L(P)\) is the space of affine functions. Every compatible
section therefore consists of points \(p_-\in\rho T\), \(p_0\in T\),
\(p_+\in\rho T\) satisfying
\[
 p_0=(p_-+p_+)/2. \tag{7}
\]
Let \(D_z\) be the actual, unnormalized, within-fiber halfspace depth of
\(p_z\). We will prove the uniform strict upper bound
\[
 \boxed{\quad D_-+D_0+D_+
       \le\gamma_d M-\frac{c\gamma_d(1-\rho)}{d}.
       \quad} \tag{8}
\]
Thus every compatible section loses a fixed positive part of the full
local Grünbaum budget.

### A simplex cap estimate

For \(p\in sT\), write its barycentric coordinates as
\(\lambda_0=1-\sum_i p_i/s\) and \(\lambda_i=p_i/s\), \(1\le i\le d\).
Put \(m=\max_i\lambda_i\ge1/(d+1)\). The closed cap
\(\{\lambda_i\ge\lambda_i(p)\}\), for an index attaining \(m\),
contains \(p\) and has volume \(s^d c(1-m)^d\). Therefore
\[
 D_{sT}(p)\le s^d c(1-m)^d. \tag{9}
\]
For \(m\in[1/(d+1),1]\), the concave function
\(\gamma_d-(1-m)^d\) lies above the chord between its endpoint values
zero and \(\gamma_d\). (For \(d=1\) it is linear.) Hence
\[
 \gamma_d-(1-m)^d
 \ge\frac{\gamma_d(d+1)}{d}\left(m-\frac1{d+1}\right). \tag{10}
\]
Let \(L(p)=\sum_i p_i\), and let
\(E_s(p)=L(p)-ds/(d+1)\). If this quantity is nonnegative, one of
\(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d\) is at least
\(1/(d+1)+E_s(p)/(ds)\). If it is negative, \(\lambda_0\) is at least
\(1/(d+1)+|E_s(p)|/s\). In both cases
\[
 m-\frac1{d+1}\ge\frac{|E_s(p)|}{ds}. \tag{11}
\]
Combining (9)-(11) gives the quantitative depth deficit
\[
 \gamma_d s^d c-D_{sT}(p)
 \ge \frac{c\gamma_d(d+1)}{d^2}s^{d-1}|E_s(p)|. \tag{12}
\]

### Applying the affine compatibility equation

Set
\[
 E_0=L(p_0)-\frac d{d+1},\qquad
 E_\pm=L(p_\pm)-\frac{d\rho}{d+1},\qquad
 A=\frac{d(1-\rho)}{d+1}>0.
\]
Equation (7) implies
\[
 E_0=(E_-+E_+)/2-A,
\]
so the triangle inequality yields
\[
 |E_0|+\frac{|E_-|+|E_+|}{2}\ge A. \tag{13}
\]
The parameter choice ensures \(2\rho^{d-1}\ge1\): this is immediate
for \(d=1\), and for \(d>1\) follows from
\(\rho>2^{-1/d}\). Consequently
\[
 |E_0|+\rho^{d-1}(|E_-|+|E_+|)\ge A.
\]
Sum (12) for the three fibers and substitute this inequality. The total
deficit is at least
\[
 \frac{c\gamma_d(d+1)}{d^2}A
       =\frac{c\gamma_d(1-\rho)}d,
\]
which proves (8).

For a fully rational planar instance, choose \(d=2\), \(\rho=3/4\).
Then \(M=17c/8\), \(\gamma_2M=17c/18\), and (8) reads
\[
 D_-+D_0+D_+\le\frac{8c}{9}
               =\gamma_2M-\frac c{18}.
\]
Every parameter, body vertex, and coefficient in this certificate is
rational; the proof does not appeal to numerical optimization.

## Scope of the obstruction

Equation (8) disproves the assertion that one can always choose compatible
local centers whose summed actual within-fiber depths reach
\(\gamma_d M\). It applies even to three homothetic simplices, with every
fiber nonheavy, and allows arbitrary choices of local centers.

It does not disprove the tensorization inequality itself. The weighted
centerpoint depth of a particular center graph can exceed the generic
\(1/h(P)\) fraction used in (6), and ambient halfspaces can collect
additional mass from fibers whose selected centers they miss. Neither
source of additional mass is included in the budget in (8).
